title: Continuity Brings Rebirth
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Master Shandao said: “It is precisely because chanting the Name is easy that continuity brings rebirth. If one can sustain it thought after thought, setting the limit at the end of life, then ten of ten are reborn, a hundred of a hundred are reborn. …May all people earnestly reflect: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must rouse the mind and restrain oneself, and never abandon it by day or night. inline.s: Master Shandao said: “It is precisely because chanting the Name is so easy that continuity leads to rebirth. If one can sustain it thought after thought, setting the limit at the end of life, then ten of ten are reborn, a hundred of a hundred are reborn. …May all people earnestly reflect: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must rouse the mind and restrain oneself, and not abandon it by day or night. When the previous thought reaches death’s end, the next thought is at once reborn. Eternally enjoying the unconditioned bliss of Dharma, and even attaining Buddhahood — is this not joy indeed!”

[It is precisely because chanting the Name is easy] This means that reciting the Buddha’s Name is easier to accomplish than contemplation of the Buddha’s image. [Continuity brings rebirth] At the moment of death, so long as one’s thought of Buddha-recitation remains continuous (not interrupted by deluded thoughts), one attains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Master Yinguang said:

“The practice of Buddha-recitation should take the Pure Land sutras and treatises as authoritative. Sentient beings of the Dharma-ending age have heavy karma and deep hindrances; relying on the Contemplation Sutra to practice contemplation is still hard to accomplish. Therefore most of the patriarchs of the Lotus School concentrated exclusively on reciting the Name. Because reciting the Name is easy,
continuity brings rebirth
(Letter to Layman Ding Fubao, no. 7, Collected Writings of Master Yinguang)  [One who sets the limit at the end of life] One who practices thus through his whole life.

[Rouse the mind and restrain oneself] To rouse the mind is to stir oneself to do what should be done; to restrain oneself is to keep oneself from doing what should not be done. These four characters, “rouse the mind and restrain the self,” are a mighty weapon for overcoming hardship and sweeping away obstructions.
[Never abandon it by day or night] One must not cease this thought-by-thought continuity either by day or by night.
Question:
Master Shandao taught:
“Continuity brings rebirth.”
What does this mean?
Answer: “Continuity brings rebirth” means:
when at the moment of death one’s thought of Buddha-recitation continues
(not interrupted by deluded thoughts)
, one attains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

“Continuity” here means that the thought of Buddha-recitation follows thought after thought, without any deluded thought mixed in (if a deluded thought is mixed in, it is no longer continuity). One must not misunderstand the two characters “continuity” here as a mere continuation of the Buddha’s Name on the lips (while deluded thoughts are mixed in the mind). As the saying goes, an error of a hair’s breadth leads astray by a thousand li.

Question: How do we know that “continuity brings rebirth” means that the thought of Buddha-recitation is continuous at the moment of death and one is thereby reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and not that so long as one’s thoughts were once continuous on ordinary days, one is reborn in the Western Land at death?
Answer: Master Shandao taught:
“If one can sustain it thought after thought,
setting the limit at the end of life
(one who practices thus through his whole life)
, then ten of ten are reborn, a hundred of a hundred are reborn.”
Please note
“setting the limit at the end of life”
, and not one who on ordinary days happened to maintain thought-by-thought continuity. Master Shandao continued to teach:
“May all people earnestly reflect: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must rouse the mind and restrain oneself, and never abandon it by day or night
(never ceasing this thought-by-thought continuity by day or night)
when the previous thought reaches death’s end, the next thought is at once reborn
. Eternally enjoying the unconditioned bliss of Dharma, and even attaining Buddhahood — is this not joy indeed!”
Therefore, “continuity brings rebirth” means that when the thought of Buddha-recitation is continuous at the moment of death, one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Question: How do we know that “continuity” in “continuity brings rebirth” refers to “the continuity of the thought of Buddha-recitation,” and not to “a continuation of the Buddha’s Name on the lips (while deluded thoughts are mixed in the mind)”?
Answer: “Continuity brings rebirth” comes from Master Shandao’s Treatise on the Special and Miscellaneous Practices of Pure Karma, which states:

Question: Why not have people contemplate, and instead directly instruct them to recite the Name exclusively? Answer: Because sentient beings have heavy obstructions, the realm is subtle while the mind is coarse, the consciousness races and the spirit flies, so contemplation is hard to accomplish. Therefore the Great Sage
(Shakyamuni Buddha)
in his compassionate pity directly urged them to recite the Name alone.
It is precisely because chanting the Name is easy
(that is, because reciting the Name is easier to accomplish than contemplation of the Buddha’s image)
that continuity brings rebirth
(at the moment of death, so long as one’s thought of Buddha-recitation remains continuous (not interrupted by deluded thoughts), one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)
. If one can sustain it thought after thought, setting the limit at the end of life
(one who practices thus through his whole life)
, then ten of ten are reborn, a hundred of a hundred are reborn.
Why is this? Because there is no stray external distraction,
one gains right mindfulness
(because the mind does not reach out in a scattered way to all sorts of objects, and so gains right mindfulness),

which accords with the Buddha’s original vow, does not go against the teaching, and follows the Buddha’s words. But if one abandons single-minded recitation and practices mixed karma, he will barely find one or two in a hundred, three or four in a thousand. Why? Because the scattered distractions confound him
(because the mind reaches out in a scattered way to all sorts of objects),
he loses right mindfulness,
which does not accord with the Buddha’s original vow, goes against the teaching, and does not follow the Buddha’s words, because
his mindfulness is not continuous
his mind is not continuous in mindful gratitude for the Buddha’s grace

, and though he performs karmic practices they always accord with fame and gain; he delights in approaching scattered distractions, and obstructs his own and others’ right practice of rebirth. May all people earnestly reflect: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must rouse the mind and restrain oneself, and never abandon it by day or night,
when the previous thought reaches death’s end, the next thought is at once reborn
. Eternally enjoying the unconditioned bliss of Dharma, and even attaining Buddhahood — is this not joy indeed!”
(from the Treatise on the Special and Miscellaneous Practices of Pure Karma by Master Shandao of the Tang Dynasty; its annotation is detailed in
Master Shandao’s Pure Land Teachings
, a passage)

Please note what Master Shandao said in this discourse: “thought after thought continuous,” “gaining right mindfulness,” “losing right mindfulness,” “mindfulness not continuous,” “mind not continuous,” “when the previous thought reaches death’s end, the next thought is at once reborn.” All of these show that “continuity” in “continuity brings rebirth” means “the thought of Buddha-recitation, continuous thought after thought,” and not “the Buddha’s Name continued on the lips (while deluded thoughts are mixed in the mind).”
Master Yinguang greatly admired this discourse, saying

“Venerable Shandao is an incarnation of Amitabha Buddha; he possesses great transcendent powers and great wisdom. In propagating the Pure Land he did not esteem the mysterious and subtle, but only taught people to practice in a genuine, plain, and practical way.
As for the special and mixed practices he set forth, their benefit is inexhaustible.
(Letter to a certain layman of Yongjia and his brothers, Collected Writings of Master Yinguang)
Master Tanluan said:
with no other thought mixed in
(that is, with no other thought intermingled)
, thought following thought, up to ten thoughts,
this is called the continuity of the ten thoughts
(Treatise on the Meaning of the Pure Land of Peace and Bliss, in Brief) Therefore,
continuity means no other thought mixed in
(that is, with no other thought intermingled).
Master Daochuo said:

“When all sentient beings are at the point of death, the knife-wind dissolves the body, the suffering of death presses upon them, and great terror arises. Therefore, encountering a good spiritual friend, they rouse great valor and reach
thought after thought, mindful continuity
through ten thoughts — this is the superior root of good, and they then attain rebirth.”
(The Collection on Peace and Bliss) Therefore,
continuity is continuity of mind upon mind, not continuity on the lips
Concerning “thought after thought continuous,” Master Yongming, the reappearance of Amitabha Buddha,
instructed:
“When walking the path
(walking meditation)
and bowing in reverence, when reciting the Buddha’s name and making vows, with fervent earnestness and single-hearted sincerity,
free of sundry thoughts
, as one going to execution, as one in prison
(a prison: a jail)

, pursued by robbers and enemies, pressed by water and fire, single-mindedly seeking rescue, wishing to escape the wheel of suffering, quickly to realize the unborn, to broadly deliver sentient beings, to uphold and spread the Three Jewels, vowing to repay the four kindnesses — with such sincerity one will surely not be disappointed. But if word and deed do not accord, and the power of faith is slight, and one has no
thought of thought-by-thought continuity
but a mind given to repeated interruption
(the thought of Buddha-recitation is interrupted by deluded thoughts)
, then relying on such negligence and hoping for rebirth at death, one is only blocked by karmic hindrances and is unlikely to meet a good spiritual friend
(that is, unlikely to meet a good teacher able to rouse his right mindfulness at the moment of death)
; wind and fire press upon him, and right mindfulness is not accomplished. Why?
The present is the cause; the moment of death is the fruit.
The cause must be real for the fruit not to be false. If one wishes
the ten thoughts of the death-moment to be accomplished
, one should prepare in advance the ferry and bridge — amass merit and dedicate it to that moment
(dedicating it to the moment of death)
, thought after thought without lapse
(accomplishing thought-by-thought continuity)
, and then there is nothing to worry about.”
(The Collection of All Good Deeds Returning to One)

In this discourse Master Yongming clearly points out: “having no thought of thought-by-thought continuity but a mind given to repeated interruption” is “word and deed not according, the power of faith slight,” that is, negligence. Therefore,
continuity is thought-by-thought continuity in the mind
, not continuity on the lips

[The ten thoughts of the death-moment to be accomplished] To accomplish the continuity of the ten thoughts at the moment of death. [Preparing the ferry and bridge] “Ferry and bridge” means a ferry crossing and a bridge. “Preparing the ferry and bridge” means making preparations in advance.
Master Chewu, the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school, taught:
“What is called upholding the Name is that of clasping it closely and keeping it in the heart —
(holding it firmly in mind) —
that is, to hold it firmly in the mind without a moment’s forgetting. Should there be
the slightest interruption of a single thought
, then it is not upholding. Should there be
the slightest intermingling of a single thought
, then it is not upholding.
Thought after thought continuous, without intermingling or interruption,
that is true diligence. With diligence unceasing, one gradually enters single-minded, undisturbed concentration and perfectly accomplishes the Pure Land karma.”

(Posthumous Collection of Master Chewu) This means: when the thought of Buddha-recitation is not interrupted by deluded thoughts and has no deluded thought mixed in, it is called thought-by-thought continuity.
Therefore,
thought-by-thought continuity means having no deluded thought mixed in.
[Clasping closely and keeping it in the heart (
ying

)] “Clasping closely” (quan quan) means to grip without letting go, extended to earnestness; “keeping in the heart” (fu ying) means to hold firmly in mind. “Clasping closely and keeping it in the heart” describes earnestly and firmly remembering without ever forgetting.
As for what is called the continuity of the ten thoughts, in the Treatise on the Meaning of the Pure Land of Peace and Bliss, in Brief, Master Tanluan taught (see in detail
Master Tanluan’s Pure Land Teachings
, a passage):

[For example, there is a person in an empty, remote place who encounters a robber and an enemy who draws a blade and rushes straight at him to kill him. The person runs with all his might until he sees a river before him; if he can cross the river, his head and body will be safe. At that time he thinks only of the expedient of crossing: “When I reach the riverbank, shall I cross with my clothes on? Or shall I cross with my clothes off? If I keep my clothes on, I fear I may not get across; if I take my clothes off, I fear I may not have time.” He has only this thought and no other concern; the single thought of how to cross the river — this alone is the one thought.
With a mind thus unstirred by other thoughts, it is called the continuity of the ten thoughts.

Answer: For example, a person in the open wilderness meets a robber and an enemy who draws a blade and charges at him to kill him. The person flees for his life and sees a great river; if he can cross this river, he can keep his life intact. At that time the only thing he thinks of is how best to cross: “When I reach the riverbank, shall I swim across with my clothes on, or with my clothes off? If with my clothes on, I fear I may not make it across; if with my clothes off, I fear there may be no time.” At such a moment he has only the thought of crossing the river, nothing else — the single thought of how to cross. Thus, without any other thought mixed in, it is called the continuity of the ten thoughts.
[The practitioner is likewise. Thinking of Amitabha Buddha, just as that person thought of crossing, he goes straight
(meaning “directly”),

through the ten thoughts: whether recollecting the Buddha’s name, recollecting the Buddha’s marks and features, recollecting the Buddha’s light, recollecting the Buddha’s spiritual powers, recollecting the Buddha’s merits, recollecting the Buddha’s wisdom, or recollecting the Buddha’s original vow.
With no other thought mixed in, thought following thought, up to ten thoughts, it is called the continuity of the ten thoughts.

The practitioner likewise, single-mindedly thinking of Amitabha Buddha, just as that person single-mindedly thought of how to cross the river, goes straight through ten thoughts: recollecting the Buddha’s name, recollecting the Buddha’s marks and features, recollecting the Buddha’s light, recollecting the Buddha’s spiritual powers, recollecting the Buddha’s merits, recollecting the Buddha’s wisdom, recollecting the Buddha’s original vow. With no other thought mixed in, thought following thought, up to ten thoughts, it is called the continuity of the ten thoughts.
[Following one after another] One thought following the next.
Question: What does “when the previous thought reaches death’s end, the next thought is at once reborn” mean?

Answer: This means that because of thought-by-thought continuity, the last thought at the moment of death is necessarily a thought of Buddha-recitation, and immediately after that last thought one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Question: It is said that Master Shandao maintained that reciting the Name surely brings rebirth — indeed, that he maintained “as long as there is faith, at the end of life one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.” Is this so?
Answer: As for how one gains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, Master Shandao made it completely clear in the discourse above:
“Continuity brings rebirth
(at the moment of death, so long as one’s thought of Buddha-recitation remains continuous (not interrupted by deluded thoughts), one attains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)
And he admonished:
“If one can sustain it thought after thought, setting the limit at the end of life
(one who practices thus through his whole life)
, then ten of ten are reborn, a hundred of a hundred are reborn.
May all people earnestly reflect: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must rouse the mind and restrain oneself, and never abandon it by day or night.”
This is the program of practice of the Pure Land school!

How is this maintaining that reciting the Name surely brings rebirth, or even that “as long as there is faith, at the end of life one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss”? Moreover, according to records, in his life Master Shandao copied the Amitabha Sutra in over a hundred thousand scrolls, which shows that he greatly reverenced the Amitabha Sutra and put its teaching into practice. In this sutra the Buddha says that with faith and vow, reciting the Name in single-minded, undisturbed concentration, at the end of life one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. How could Master Shandao have gone against the Buddha’s instruction and said “reciting the Name surely brings rebirth,” or even “as long as there is faith, at the end of life one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss”? Therefore,

“Master Shandao maintained that reciting the Name surely brings rebirth; Master Shandao maintained that as long as there is faith, at the end of life one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; …” — all such claims are fabricated by later people and foisted upon Master Shandao, falsely presented as his Pure Land thought. In fact, you need only compare Master Shandao’s discourse on “continuity brings rebirth” and his discourse on the “special and assisting practices” with those so-called “Pure Land ideas of Master Shandao,” and you will clearly see that, under the banner of “relying on Master Shandao,” these people are in fact opposing him head-on by taking his words out of context and twisting his original text.

Question: Since these people do not truly believe in Master Shandao, why do they raise the banner of “relying on Master Shandao” and say that “the moment faith arises, one is reborn,” “reciting the Name surely brings rebirth,” “the gate of the great vow,” and such things are his Pure Land thought?

Answer: Because such statements as “the moment faith arises, one is reborn,” “reciting the Name surely brings rebirth,” and “the gate of the great vow” — if people knew these were the speakers’ own words, since they plainly depart from the meaning of the scriptures, people would turn up their noses in contempt and no one would believe them. But if they take Master Shandao’s original text out of context and twist it, and falsely claim this is his Pure Land thought, and go on to say: “Since Master Shandao is an incarnation of Amitabha Buddha, his thought
is no different from what Amitabha Buddha personally proclaimed.”
Then they can deceive the faithful, and no one dares to criticize or oppose them.
Question: What are
the “special and assisting practices”?
Answer: This is Master Shandao’s discourse on
how the Pure Land school should practice. The Master said
By “special practice” is meant one who practices relying exclusively on the rebirth-promoting sutras; this is called special practice. What are these?
Single-mindedly
reciting this Contemplation Sutra, the Amitabha Sutra, the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, and the like,
single-mindedly
contemplating, observing, and recollecting the twofold adornments of that land. If bowing, then
single-mindedly
bow to that Buddha alone; if chanting aloud, then
single-mindedly
chant that Buddha’s name alone; if praising and making offerings, then
single-mindedly
praise and make offerings alone; this is called “special.” Moreover, within this special practice there are again two kinds: first,
single-mindedly

mindful of the name of Amitabha Buddha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, regardless of time or duration, never abandoning it thought after thought — this is called the karma of right concentration, because it accords with that Buddha’s vow; if relying on bowing, reciting, and so on, this is called assisting karma. Apart from these special and assisting practices, all other good deeds are called mixed practices. If one cultivates the aforementioned special and assisting practices, with the mind always drawing near and recollecting without cease, this is called “uninterrupted.””
Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra in Four Fascicles

Translation: Yet there are two kinds of practice: first, special practice; second, mixed practice. “Special practice” means one who practices relying exclusively on the rebirth-promoting sutras (the Sutra of the Contemplation of Immeasurable Life, the Amitabha Sutra, and the Sutra of Immeasurable Life); this is special practice. What are these? Single-mindedly, with focused attention, reciting the Sutra of the Contemplation of Immeasurable Life, the Amitabha Sutra, the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, and the like; single-mindedly, with focused attention, contemplating, observing, and recollecting the twofold adornments of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. If bowing to the Buddha, then single-mindedly, with focused attention, bow to Amitabha Buddha; if chanting aloud, then single-mindedly, with focused attention, chant the name of Amitabha Buddha; if praising and making offerings, then single-mindedly, with focused attention, praise and make offerings — only then is it called special practice. Moreover, within this special practice there are again two kinds: first, single-mindedly, with focused attention, mindfully reciting the name of Amitabha Buddha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, regardless of time or duration, never abandoning it thought after thought (the thought of Buddha-recitation flowing onward unbroken — not severed by sundry thoughts); this is called the karma of right concentration, because it accords with the original vow of Amitabha Buddha; if relying on bowing, praising, making offerings, and the like, this is called assisting karma. Apart from these two special and assisting practices, all other good deeds are called mixed practice. If one cultivates these special and assisting practices, with the mind always drawing near to Amitabha Buddha and recollecting without cease, it is called “uninterrupted” (without deluded thoughts mixed in).
In this discourse Master Shandao lays great emphasis on
single-mindedness
; whether reciting sutras, recollecting, bowing to the Buddha, reciting the Name, or praising and making offerings,
one must all
be single-minded
, for this is
the key
to correct practice!
Single-mindedness
means thought following thought, without another thought mixed in.
Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, in his Rebirth Treatise, says:
World-Honored One, I
single-mindedly
take refuge in the Tathagata of Unobstructed Light throughout the ten directions, and wish to be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.”
Master Tanluan, in his Commentary on the Rebirth Treatise, explains:
“I
single-mindedly” —
these are the words Bodhisattva Vasubandhu used to exhort himself, meaning: mindful of the Tathagata of Unobstructed Light, wishing to be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss,
thought following thought, without another thought mixed in
Therefore, “single-mindedness” means thought following thought, without another thought mixed in.
[Unobstructed Light Tathagata] One of the twelve names of Amitabha Buddha.
Master Zhiyi said:
“If one applies the mind and keeps it in mind,
thought after thought continuous,
with no other thought interrupting
(not interrupted by any other thought)
this is called single-mindedness.”
(Commentary on the Meaning of the Avalokiteshvara Chapter)
Single-mindedness means focusing the mind wholly on one thing, without a second thought;
this is also what Master Yongming, the reappearance of Amitabha Buddha, expressed by “
free of sundry thoughts
(without any other thought).” Master Yongming said:
“When walking the path
(walking meditation)
and bowing in reverence, when reciting the Buddha’s name and making vows, with fervent earnestness and single-hearted sincerity,
free of sundry thoughts
, as one going to execution, as one in prison
(a prison: a jail)
, pursued by robbers and enemies, pressed by water and fire,
single-mindedly

seeking rescue, wishing to escape the wheel of suffering, quickly to realize the unborn, to broadly deliver sentient beings, to uphold and spread the Three Jewels, vowing to repay the four kindnesses. With such sincerity one will surely not be disappointed.”

(Translation: When walking the path and bowing in reverence, when reciting the Buddha’s name and making vows, with earnest sincerity, without sundry thoughts, as one about to be executed, as one imprisoned, as one pursued by robbers, as one pressed by water and fire, earnestly
single-mindedly

seeking rescue, wishing to escape the wheel of suffering, quickly to realize the unborn, to broadly deliver sentient beings, to uphold and spread the Three Jewels, vowing to repay the four kindnesses. With such sincerity the merit is not in vain, and one will surely be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.)
(The Collection of All Good Deeds Returning to One)

[The wheel of suffering] The bitter fruits of birth and death turn like a wheel without ceasing. [The unborn] Neither arising nor ceasing, which is the principle of nirvana. [To uphold and spread] To carry on and spread. [Sincere] Deeply sincere and single-hearted.
Question: Why did Master Shandao copy the Amitabha Sutra in over a hundred thousand scrolls?

Answer: In those days the art of printing did not yet exist, so all sutra scrolls were hand-copied and therefore rare and precious. Master Shandao, so that the broad mass of Buddha-reciters could practice in accordance with the Amitabha Sutra as the Buddha taught — with faith and vow, reciting the Name in single-minded, undisturbed concentration — copied them and distributed them to the reciters. This also proves that Master Shandao did not maintain that “as long as there is faith, at the end of life one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss”; rather, he maintained that reciters should practice according to the Amitabha Sutra as the Buddha taught: with faith and vow, reciting the Name in single-minded, undisturbed concentration, at the end of life one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. The fourfold assembly, moved by his transforming influence, turned their minds to the Pure Land in countless numbers. Among Master Shandao’s disciples there were those who recited the Amitabha Sutra from one hundred thousand to five hundred thousand times, and those who recited the Buddha’s name as a daily practice from ten thousand to one hundred thousand times; of those who thereby attained the samadhi of Buddha-recitation and accomplished rebirth in the Pure Land, none could be fully recounted.
Question: When a Buddha-reciter dies, Amitabha Buddha will naturally send a boat to meet him — why is single-minded, undisturbed concentration necessary?

Answer: When a Buddha-reciter dies, seven boats come to meet him: one is the boat to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and the other six are respectively the boats to the deva realm, the human realm, the asura realm, the animal realm, the hungry ghost realm, and the hell realm. The reason Buddha-recitation requires single-minded, undisturbed concentration is so that at the moment of death one’s right mindfulness is clear and one boards the boat bound for the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Therefore Master Shandao taught that one should
sustain it thought after thought, setting the limit at the end of life
. If one can accomplish
thought after thought, setting the limit at the end of life
, then
when the previous thought reaches death’s end, the next thought is at once reborn

. If at the moment of death one is enveloped by errant thoughts, then amid those delusions, drawn by the force of karma, one boards the boat corresponding to one’s own karma among the six realms. (This is what Master Yongming — the reappearance of Amitabha Buddha, sixth patriarch of the Pure Land school — said in his Four Alternatives: “When the phantom realm suddenly appears before you, in a blink you follow it away.”) If at death one recites the Buddha’s name without errant thoughts or lethargy, then the power of the vow takes charge and one boards the boat to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; this is precisely the situation Master Shandao described as
when the previous thought reaches death’s end, the next thought is at once reborn
. So Master Shandao earnestly admonished:
“May all people earnestly reflect: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must rouse the mind and restrain oneself, and never abandon it by day or night”
, and then it will be:
“when the previous thought reaches death’s end, the next thought is at once reborn. Eternally enjoying the unconditioned bliss of Dharma, and even attaining Buddhahood — is this not joy indeed!”

This is also why Master Shandao copied the Amitabha Sutra in over a hundred thousand scrolls and distributed it to reciters, so that they might practice according to the Amitabha Sutra as the Buddha taught and attain single-minded, undisturbed concentration in reciting the Buddha’s name. In this way, at the moment of death, one is not enveloped by errant thoughts but, with clear right mindfulness, boards the boat bound for the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Question: The moment faith arises, one is reborn. Where is right mindfulness at the moment of death needed?
Answer: How could right mindfulness at the moment of death not be needed? Master Shandao taught:
“When one is gravely ill and about to die, his close relatives must not shed tears and wail, nor raise sounds of sighing and regret that would confuse and disturb his mind,
making him lose right mindfulness
. Rather, they should all recite the Buddha’s name in unison, and only when his breath has ceased may they weep and mourn.
If there is the slightest thought of attachment to the world, it becomes a hindrance and one cannot attain liberation.

If one can meet a person who understands the Pure Land and come repeatedly to encourage him, this is an extremely great fortune. If one acts accordingly, he is certain to transcend the cycle and be reborn, with no doubt about it.”
Venerable Shandao’s Essay on Right Mindfulness for Rebirth at the Moment of Death
) In this Essay on Right Mindfulness for Rebirth at the Moment of Death, Master Shandao continued to teach:

Monks, laypeople, and even those who have not practiced Buddha-recitation, if they use this method, all attain rebirth — of this there is no doubt. I have often seen worldly people who, in their ordinary days, are diligent and fervent in reciting the Buddha’s name, bowing in praise, and vowing to be reborn in the West.
(most earnest and sincere)
Yet when they fall ill, they again fear death and speak no more of rebirth and liberation. Only after their breath has faded and their life is spent,
when their consciousness has plunged into the dark realm,
do they at last begin the ten thoughts. This is precisely like closing the door after the thief has gone — what use is it? The matter of death and birth is momentous;
one must exert oneself by one’s own effort.
If a single thought goes astray, one suffers for kalpas upon kalpas — who can take one’s place? Think of it! Think of it! When one has no urgent matter, one should
diligently accept and uphold this method
; this is the great matter of the moment of death.”
From this Essay on Right Mindfulness for Rebirth at the Moment of Death, we can clearly see the guiding thought of Master Shandao’s Pure Land practice:
1. To be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one must have right mindfulness at the moment of death; hence the title of the essay is
Right Mindfulness for Rebirth at the Moment of Death
2. In order to
be able to ensure right mindfulness at the moment of death,
one must cultivate diligently in ordinary days,
accomplishing thought-by-thought continuity;
this is the foremost great matter of the Buddha-reciter.
Therefore, Master Shandao was by no means maintaining that “as long as a Buddha-reciter has faith, at the end of life one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.” Rather he maintained:

“Because chanting the Name is easy, continuity brings rebirth. If one can sustain it thought after thought, setting the limit at the end of life, then ten of ten are reborn, a hundred of a hundred are reborn.

May all people earnestly reflect: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must rouse the mind and restrain oneself, and never abandon it by day or night — when the previous thought reaches death’s end, the next thought is at once reborn. Eternally enjoying the unconditioned bliss of Dharma, and even attaining Buddhahood — is this not joy indeed!”
It is precisely because of “thought after thought, setting the limit at the end of life” that one can ensure right mindfulness at death and at once gain rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Question: Master Shandao, in his Commentary on the Sutra of the Contemplation of Immeasurable Life (the Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra in Four Fascicles), says:

“Single-mindedly mindful of the name of Amitabha Buddha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, regardless of time or duration, never abandoning it thought after thought — this is called the karma of right concentration, because it accords with that Buddha’s vow.”
What is meant by “karma of right concentration”?
